exp: Adult-onset Still's disease is a diagnosis of exclusion (Yamaguchi criteria) — the combination of quotidian fever, evanescent salmon rash, sore throat, and very high ferritin should trigger consideration after ruling out infection and malignancy.

subject: Medicine
q: A 7-year-old child presents 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat with migratory polyarthritis of large joints, a new pansystolic murmur at the apex, and subcutaneous nodules over the extensor surfaces. ESR and ASO titer are elevated. Which diagnostic criteria are used to establish this diagnosis?
why: Wrong — Duke criteria diagnose infective endocarditis.
Wrong — Light's criteria classify pleural effusion.
Wrong — Ranson's criteria assess pancreatitis severity.
Correct — Jones criteria (revised) diagnose acute rheumatic fever using evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus major and minor criteria.
exp: Jones criteria (revised 2015, with population risk-stratification) diagnose acute rheumatic fever; India uses the moderate/high-risk criteria threshold — secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin then prevents progression to rheumatic heart disease.

subject: Medicine
q: Which mnemonic summarizes the indications for emergency haemodialysis in severe acute kidney injury?
why: FAST is unrelated, used for stroke recognition or trauma ultrasound
Correct — AEIOU is the standard emergency dialysis mnemonic
SOAP is a clinical documentation format, not a dialysis mnemonic
ABCDE is the primary trauma survey, not dialysis indications
exp: AEIOU — refractory Acidosis, Electrolyte abnormalities (severe hyperkalemia), Intoxication with a dialyzable toxin, fluid Overload refractory to diuretics, and Uremic symptoms (encephalopathy, pericarditis) — summarizes the classic indications for emergency dialysis in acute kidney injury.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is found to have splenomegaly and neutropenia on routine evaluation. What is this triad called?
why: Sjögren syndrome is sicca symptoms with anti-Ro/La antibodies, a different RA-associated entity
Caplan syndrome is rheumatoid arthritis with pneumoconiotic pulmonary nodules
Correct — rheumatoid arthritis plus splenomegaly plus neutropenia defines Felty syndrome
Still's disease is a systemic inflammatory arthritis with quotidian fever and salmon-coloured rash
exp: Felty syndrome is the triad of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia seen in long-standing severe RA, carrying an increased risk of serious bacterial infection; management targets the underlying RA, with splenectomy reserved for refractory cytopenia or recurrent infection.

subject: Medicine
q: In a patient with severe aortic regurgitation, a soft mid-diastolic rumbling murmur is heard at the cardiac apex. What is this murmur called?
why: Graham Steell murmur is an early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension
Carey Coombs murmur is a mid-diastolic murmur of active rheumatic carditis/mitral valvulitis
Still's murmur is an innocent childhood systolic murmur, unrelated to aortic regurgitation
Correct — an apical mid-diastolic rumble in severe aortic regurgitation is the Austin Flint murmur
exp: An Austin Flint murmur is a soft, low-pitched mid-diastolic (or presystolic) rumble at the apex in severe aortic regurgitation, caused by the regurgitant jet impinging on the anterior mitral leaflet and functionally narrowing the mitral orifice; it must be distinguished from true mitral stenosis.

subject: Medicine
q: Which serological test is the preferred initial screening investigation for suspected celiac disease in a patient with normal total IgA levels?
why: Correct — anti-tTG IgA antibody is the standard first-line serological screening test for celiac disease
Anti-gliadin antibodies are less sensitive/specific and largely superseded by tTG testing
Anti-mitochondrial antibody is specific for primary biliary cholangitis, unrelated to celiac disease
Anti-smooth muscle antibody is associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not celiac disease
exp: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA antibody is the preferred initial screening test for celiac disease given its high sensitivity and specificity in IgA-sufficient patients; IgA deficiency requires total IgA measurement alongside it or IgG-based testing, with duodenal biopsy remaining confirmatory.

subject: Medicine
q: Which viral hepatitis carries the highest risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality when acquired in the third trimester of pregnancy?
why: Hepatitis A can rarely cause fulminant failure but lacks HEV's pregnancy-specific mortality risk
Correct — Hepatitis E in the third trimester carries the highest fulminant hepatic failure and mortality risk among viral hepatitides
Hepatitis B in pregnancy is more notable for perinatal transmission risk than fulminant failure
Hepatitis C rarely causes acute fulminant hepatitis
exp: Hepatitis E virus infection, though usually self-limiting, carries a markedly elevated risk of fulminant hepatic failure and maternal mortality (up to 20-25%) when acquired in the third trimester, making it an important cause of severe acute hepatitis in pregnant women in endemic settings including India.

subject: Medicine
q: A woman who had severe postpartum haemorrhage several weeks earlier now presents with failure of lactation and amenorrhea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Postpartum thyroiditis presents with thyroid dysfunction, not failed lactation from pituitary necrosis
Lymphocytic hypophysitis is autoimmune pituitary inflammation, not specifically tied to haemorrhagic shock
Correct — postpartum haemorrhage followed by failed lactation is the classic presentation of Sheehan syndrome
Empty sella syndrome is often an incidental imaging finding, not typically presenting acutely with agalactia after haemorrhage
exp: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis from severe obstetric haemorrhage and hypotension, to which the physiologically enlarged pituitary of pregnancy is especially vulnerable; the earliest and most characteristic feature is failure of lactation from loss of prolactin, followed by amenorrhea and variable pituitary hormone deficiency.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with long-standing diabetic nephropathy has persistent hyperkalemia with a mild normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, in the setting of hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is this?
why: Type 1 (distal) RTA causes hypokalemia, nephrocalcinosis/stones, and inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5
Type 2 (proximal) RTA causes hypokalemia from bicarbonate wasting, as in Fanconi syndrome
Type 3 RTA is a rare mixed variant, not the classic diabetic-nephropathy pattern
Correct — hyperkalemic RTA from hypoaldosteronism in diabetic nephropathy is type 4
exp: Type 4 RTA results from hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy, and is characterized by hyperkalemia with a mild normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, distinguishing it from the hypokalemic type 1 and type 2 RTAs.

subject: Medicine
q: What is the standard first-line eradication regimen for Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease?
opts: PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin for 14 days
Amoxicillin plus metronidazole without a PPI
H2 receptor blocker plus clarithromycin alone
why: Correct among these options — PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin triple therapy — though bismuth-based quadruple therapy is now India's actual first-line regimen per the Bhubaneswar Consensus
PPI monotherapy does not eradicate H. pylori
Omitting the PPI significantly reduces eradication efficacy
H2 blockers are weaker acid suppressants than PPIs for eradication regimens
exp: Classical PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin triple therapy for 14 days is still widely taught, but the Indian Society of Gastroenterology's 2021 Bhubaneswar Consensus now recommends bismuth-based quadruple therapy as the actual first-line regimen in India, since pooled Indian clarithromycin resistance (~23%) exceeds the 15% threshold above which triple therapy becomes unreliable (Maastricht V/VI).

subject: Medicine
q: A previously healthy 30-year-old man with a family history of sudden cardiac death is found to have coved-type ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V3, with a structurally normal heart on echocardiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome shows a short PR interval with a delta wave, a different ECG pattern
Correct — coved ST elevation in V1-V3 with a structurally normal heart defines Brugada syndrome
Long QT syndrome shows a prolonged QT interval, not coved ST elevation
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy shows structural right ventricular abnormalities on imaging, unlike the normal echo here
exp: Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiac sodium-channelopathy (commonly SCN5A mutations) causing coved-type ST elevation in the right precordial leads in a structurally normal heart, predisposing to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and sudden death; an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is definitive treatment for high-risk patients.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old woman describes brief, recurrent episodes of severe, electric shock-like pain over the right side of her face, triggered by chewing and light touch, with a normal neurological examination between episodes. What is the first-line drug for this condition?
why: Amitriptyline is used for chronic neuropathic pain/migraine prophylaxis, not first-line for trigeminal neuralgia
Phenytoin is a second-line option, not first-line
Correct — carbamazepine is the first-line drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia
Sumatriptan is used for acute migraine, not trigeminal neuralgia
exp: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by brief, paroxysmal, electric shock-like unilateral facial pain triggered by innocuous stimuli along a trigeminal nerve division, with a normal examination between attacks; carbamazepine is the established first-line drug, with microvascular decompression reserved for refractory cases.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old presents with recurrent painful erythema and swelling of both external ears that spares the earlobes, together with a saddle-nose deformity and new hoarseness of voice. Which autoimmune condition targets cartilage in this pattern?
why: This correctly identifies the cartilage-specific, lobule-sparing pattern as diagnostic
GPA causes saddle-nose from necrotizing granulomatous destruction plus renal/pulmonary involvement and is c-ANCA/PR3-associated, not primarily recurrent auricular chondritis
Cogan syndrome combines interstitial keratitis with vestibuloauditory symptoms, not this cartilage pattern
Sarcoidosis can cause lupus pernio of nasal skin, not cartilage destruction, and does not spare the earlobe in this way
exp: Relapsing polychondritis is an autoimmune attack on cartilaginous structures - auricular cartilage (sparing the lobule, which has no cartilage), nasal septal cartilage (saddle nose), and laryngotracheal cartilage (hoarseness/airway compromise) - and can be life-threatening if the airway is involved.

subject: Medicine
q: A 22-year-old with palpitations has an ECG showing a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave). He is given IV verapamil for presumed SVT and rapidly deteriorates into an irregular wide-complex tachycardia. What was the error in management?
opts: No error - verapamil is appropriate first-line therapy for any narrow-complex tachycardia
The management was correct; the verapamil dose should simply be increased
This is ordinary AV nodal reentrant tachycardia, so an AV-nodal blocker was the safe choice
AV-nodal blockade in pre-excited atrial fibrillation preferentially conducts down the accessory pathway, risking ventricular fibrillation
why: Verapamil is not safe here - the ECG already shows WPW (delta wave), not an ordinary narrow-complex tachycardia needing routine AV-nodal blockade
Increasing the dose of a contraindicated drug worsens the risk rather than fixing the error
The delta wave and short PR interval already establish WPW with pre-excited conduction, not ordinary AVNRT
This correctly explains why AV-nodal blockade is dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation
exp: In WPW, if the patient develops atrial fibrillation (pre-excited AF), AV-nodal blocking drugs (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine) block the normal AV node but not the accessory pathway, paradoxically increasing conduction down the bypass tract and precipitating VF; correct management is procainamide/ibutilide or DC cardioversion if unstable.

subject: Medicine
q: A 60-year-old develops sudden vertigo, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, hoarseness, and dysphagia after a posterior circulation stroke. Occlusion of which artery best explains this constellation?
why: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and tongue deviation, a different pattern
MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiparesis/hemisensory loss with cortical signs, not this crossed brainstem pattern
This correctly identifies PICA occlusion producing lateral medullary syndrome
Basilar artery occlusion typically causes locked-in syndrome or bilateral findings, not this unilateral crossed pattern
exp: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, classically from PICA (or vertebral artery) occlusion, damaging the spinothalamic tract, descending sympathetic fibers, and nucleus ambiguus while sparing motor pathways - the crossed sensory pattern is the key discriminator from other brainstem syndromes.

subject: Medicine
q: A 30-year-old with septic shock is intubated and mechanically ventilated with PEEP of 8 cmH2O. He develops acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and no evidence of cardiac failure. On FiO2 0.5, PaO2 is 60 mmHg (P/F ratio 120). How should this be classified per the Berlin ARDS criteria?
opts: Not ARDS - this is cardiogenic pulmonary edema
why: Mild ARDS requires a P/F ratio of 200-300, higher than this patient's value
This correctly classifies a P/F ratio of 120 as moderate ARDS
Severe ARDS requires a P/F ratio below 100
Cardiac failure has been explicitly excluded, and the clinical context plus bilateral infiltrates support ARDS
exp: The Berlin definition classifies ARDS by P/F ratio on PEEP of at least 5 cmH2O: mild 200-300, moderate 100-200, severe under 100 - a P/F of 120 with bilateral infiltrates, acute onset, and exclusion of cardiac failure fits moderate ARDS.

subject: Medicine
q: A 35-year-old woman develops a painful, tender, diffusely enlarged thyroid with fever two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection; she has transient thyrotoxic symptoms, elevated ESR, and low radioactive iodine uptake. What is the diagnosis and expected course?
opts: Subacute (De Quervain) thyroiditis - self-limiting triphasic course
Graves disease - persistent hyperthyroidism requiring long-term therapy
Riedel thyroiditis - progressive fibrosis requiring surgical decompression
why: This correctly matches the painful goitre, viral prodrome, low RAIU, self-limited triphasic course
Hashimoto thyroiditis is typically painless with high anti-TPO titers and chronic progression, not a painful post-viral course
Graves disease shows high RAIU and lacks the painful post-viral pattern
Riedel thyroiditis is a rare fibrosing process causing a hard, painless woody thyroid, not an acute painful illness
exp: Subacute granulomatous (De Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral prodrome, causing a painful tender goitre, transient thyrotoxicosis with low RAIU (distinguishing it from Graves), followed by a hypothyroid phase and eventual recovery - treat pain with NSAIDs or steroids, not antithyroid drugs.

subject: Medicine
q: A 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus on eye examination; renal biopsy electron microscopy shows a basket-weave appearance of the glomerular basement membrane. What is the diagnosis and its usual inheritance pattern?
opts: Thin basement membrane disease - autosomal dominant, benign hematuria
Fabry disease - X-linked lysosomal storage disorder
why: Thin basement membrane disease causes isolated benign hematuria with a uniformly thin (not basket-weave) GBM, and no deafness/lenticonus, despite also being hereditary
Goodpasture syndrome is an anti-GBM antibody disease causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary hemorrhage, not a hereditary syndrome with deafness
Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder causing angiokeratomas and zebra bodies on EM, not basket-weave GBM
This triad with basket-weave GBM is correctly diagnostic of Alport syndrome
exp: Alport syndrome results from mutations in type IV collagen genes (most commonly COL4A5, X-linked), producing progressive nephritis, sensorineural deafness, and ocular abnormalities, with a pathognomonic basket-weave GBM on electron microscopy - a key discriminator from thin basement membrane disease.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old with chronic hepatitis B infection presents with fever, weight loss, mononeuritis multiplex, and livedo reticularis; renal angiography shows multiple microaneurysms, and ANCA testing is negative. What is the diagnosis?
why: GPA is a small-vessel, c-ANCA/PR3-associated vasculitis with sinonasal and pulmonary granulomas, not this medium-vessel angiographic pattern
Microscopic polyangiitis is p-ANCA-associated and typically spares medium vessels/does not form macroaneurysms
This correctly identifies classic PAN by its HBV association, ANCA-negative status, and medium-vessel microaneurysms
EGPA (Churg-Strauss) features asthma, eosinophilia, and p-ANCA, not this HBV-associated angiographic picture
exp: Classic polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis strongly associated with chronic hepatitis B infection, characteristically ANCA-negative, and diagnosed by angiographic microaneurysms of visceral vessels plus mononeuritis multiplex.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with a pleural effusion has a pleural fluid-to-serum protein ratio of 0.6 and a pleural fluid-to-serum LDH ratio of 0.7. Applying Light's criteria, how should this effusion be classified?
why: A transudate would have both ratios below the cutoffs (protein under 0.5, LDH under 0.6)
This correctly identifies that both ratios exceed the Light's criteria thresholds, making this an exudate
Chylothorax is diagnosed by pleural fluid triglyceride level, not Light's criteria
Hemothorax is diagnosed by pleural fluid hematocrit relative to blood, a separate test
exp: Light's criteria classify an effusion as exudative if any one is met: pleural/serum protein ratio over 0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio over 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH over two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH - this patient meets both, so a local cause should be sought.

subject: Medicine
q: A 72-year-old presents with a triad of magnetic gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline over several months; CT shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy, and gait improves temporarily after a large-volume lumbar puncture. What is the diagnosis and definitive treatment?
why: This triad with a positive tap test correctly defines NPH, treated definitively with VP shunt
Alzheimer disease shows diffuse cortical atrophy without a positive tap-test response, and gait apraxia/incontinence occur late, not early
Vascular dementia shows a stepwise decline with infarcts on imaging, not this specific triad with tap-test response
Parkinson disease dementia would show parkinsonian motor features predating the cognitive decline, not this triad
exp: NPH's classic triad (incontinence, cognitive decline, gait apraxia) with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy and improvement after a large-volume tap points to a reversible dementia treatable with VP shunting.

subject: Medicine
q: A 28-year-old with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure has an arterial pH of 7.25 despite adequate fluid resuscitation. According to King's College Criteria, does this patient meet criteria for emergency liver transplantation?
opts: Criteria apply only when grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy is already present
Arterial pH is not part of King's College Criteria
Yes - arterial pH under 7.30 after resuscitation meets King's College Criteria regardless of encephalopathy grade
why: A pH under 7.3 alone is sufficient per King's College Criteria, so medical management alone is inadequate
The pH criterion is explicitly independent of encephalopathy grade, unlike the composite criterion
Arterial pH is one of the primary King's College Criteria for paracetamol overdose
This correctly identifies that pH under 7.30 alone meets criteria for transplant listing
exp: King's College Criteria for paracetamol-induced acute liver failure list arterial pH under 7.30 (after adequate fluid resuscitation) as a standalone indication for emergency transplant listing, independent of encephalopathy grade. Flag: confirm exact cutoff values against the current reference before clinical use.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient newly diagnosed with pheochromocytoma is being prepared for adrenalectomy. Which class of antihypertensive must be started first, given the danger of starting a beta-blocker before it?
opts: Combined alpha-beta blocker given simultaneously as the first step
Alpha-blocker (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) first, followed later by a beta-blocker
A calcium channel blocker alone, with no particular sequencing needed
why: This reversed sequence risks unopposed alpha stimulation and hypertensive crisis, the exact error being tested
Combined blockade without prior alpha-blockade still carries the unopposed-alpha risk in the initial phase
This correctly identifies alpha-blockade first as the standard preoperative protocol
Calcium channel blockers can be adjuncts but do not replace the mandatory alpha-then-beta sequencing
exp: Alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade in pheochromocytoma management because starting a beta-blocker first removes the beta-2-mediated vasodilation that partially offsets catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction, leaving unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction that can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old post-operative patient develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with a Wells score indicating low probability of pulmonary embolism, and a D-dimer test is negative. What is the appropriate next step, and how would this differ if the patient had instead been high-probability?
opts: Proceed straight to thrombolysis without further imaging

No further imaging is needed - a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer excludes PE in low- and intermediate-probability patients, but a high-probability patient needs CT pulmonary angiography regardless of D-dimer
A ventilation-perfusion scan is mandatory in every patient regardless of Wells score
A positive D-dimer alone is sufficient to confirm the diagnosis of PE
why: Thrombolysis is reserved for confirmed PE with hemodynamic instability, not used empirically before diagnosis
This correctly applies the Wells-score/D-dimer algorithm across all three probability tiers
V/Q scanning is an alternative to CTPA, not a mandatory universal first step
D-dimer is highly sensitive but not specific, so a positive result requires confirmatory imaging, not diagnosis on its own
exp: In low- and intermediate-probability patients, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer has a high enough negative predictive value to exclude PE without imaging; in high-probability patients, a negative D-dimer does not reliably rule out PE, so these patients should proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography regardless of the D-dimer result.

subject: Medicine
q: What is the maximum time window from symptom onset within which IV alteplase (tPA) can be administered in eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke?
why: Wrong - too narrow, excludes eligible patients within the true window
Wrong - this was the original, now-superseded window
Correct - 4.5 hours is the current evidence-based window
Wrong - beyond 4.5 hours, IV thrombolysis is not recommended
exp: IV thrombolysis with alteplase is approved up to 4.5 hours from clearly established symptom onset in eligible patients, extended from the original 3-hour window based on the ECASS III trial, subject to standard inclusion and exclusion criteria.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with ascites has a Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) of 1.5 g/dL. This is most consistent with which cause of ascites?
why: Wrong - this classically produces a low SAAG below 1.1 g/dL
Wrong - this classically produces a low SAAG below 1.1 g/dL
Wrong - this classically produces a low SAAG below 1.1 g/dL
Correct - a SAAG of 1.5 g/dL (1.1 or above) is diagnostic of a portal-hypertensive cause
exp: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or above indicates portal-hypertensive ascites (cirrhosis, cardiac failure, Budd-Chiari) with about 97% accuracy, reflecting increased hydrostatic pressure across an intact peritoneum; a SAAG below 1.1 g/dL points to non-portal-hypertensive causes such as tuberculosis, carcinomatosis, or nephrotic syndrome.

subject: Medicine
q: As per ADA/WHO criteria, which HbA1c value is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus?
why: Correct - 6.5% or above is the diagnostic cutoff
Wrong - this is the lower threshold for prediabetes, not diabetes
Wrong - not a recognized diagnostic cutoff
Wrong - this overstates the threshold and would miss many true diabetics
exp: An HbA1c of 6.5% or above, confirmed on repeat testing or with a concordant glucose criterion, is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus; 5.7-6.4% defines prediabetes, and values below that are normal.

subject: Medicine
q: The pathognomonic skin lesion seen at the site of a chigger (mite) bite in scrub typhus is called?
why: Wrong - target lesions suggest erythema multiforme, not scrub typhus
Correct - eschar is pathognomonic of scrub typhus
Wrong - petechiae suggest a bleeding or vasculitic process, not scrub typhus specifically
Wrong - rose spots are classically described in typhoid fever, not scrub typhus
exp: The eschar - a painless, black, necrotic crust with an erythematous margin at the mite bite site - is the classic diagnostic clue for scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) and should be actively searched for in axillae, groin, and skin folds in any patient with fever of unclear source in an endemic rural setting.

subject: Medicine
q: A positive pathergy test - a papule or pustule forming at the site of a skin needle prick after 24-48 hours - is characteristically associated with which of the following conditions?
why: Wrong - pathergy is not a recognized feature of SLE
Wrong - pathergy is not a recognized feature of RA
Correct - pathergy positivity supports a diagnosis of Behcet's disease
Wrong - pathergy is not a recognized feature of Sjogren's syndrome
exp: The pathergy test, a marker of non-specific hyperreactivity of the skin to minor trauma, is a supportive diagnostic criterion for Behcet's disease, which classically also presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers and uveitis.

subject: Medicine
q: Prominent giant V waves in the jugular venous pulse are most characteristic of which valvular lesion?
why: Wrong - mitral stenosis affects the left heart and does not alter the JVP waveform directly
Wrong - aortic regurgitation produces peripheral signs like Corrigan's pulse, not giant V waves
Wrong - pulmonary stenosis may cause a prominent a wave, not a giant V wave
Correct - giant V waves are the classic JVP finding of tricuspid regurgitation
exp: In tricuspid regurgitation, blood regurgitates from the right ventricle back into the right atrium and systemic veins during ventricular systole, producing a giant fused cv (V) wave in the JVP, sometimes visible as systolic pulsation of the neck veins or earlobes.

subject: Medicine
q: What is the first-line drug of choice for initial pharmacological management of status epilepticus in an adult?
why: Correct - benzodiazepines act fastest and are recommended first-line
Wrong - appropriate as a second-line agent once a benzodiazepine has been given
Wrong - appropriate as a second-line agent once a benzodiazepine has been given
Wrong - appropriate as a second-line agent once a benzodiazepine has been given
exp: Benzodiazepines (IV lorazepam preferred, or IV/rectal/IM diazepam if unavailable) are first-line for status epilepticus due to their rapid onset of seizure termination; a second-line agent (phenytoin/fosphenytoin, valproate, or levetiracetam) is then loaded to prevent recurrence.

subject: Medicine
q: The triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhagic manifestations in a febrile patient with a history of exposure to flood water or rodent urine is classically described as?
why: Wrong - hepatorenal syndrome is a complication of advanced liver disease, unrelated to flood-water exposure
Correct - the exposure history and triad are classic for Weil's disease
Wrong - HELLP syndrome is a pregnancy-specific disorder, unrelated to flood-water exposure
Wrong - hantavirus classically causes pulmonary or renal syndromes without this specific triad
exp: Weil's disease is the severe, icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhagic manifestations, typically following exposure to water or soil contaminated with rodent urine such as flood-water exposure common in India during monsoon season; early doxycycline or penicillin plus supportive renal care are key.

subject: Medicine
q: As per WHO criteria, a DEXA scan T-score of -2.8 at the lumbar spine in a postmenopausal woman, with no history of fragility fracture, is classified as?
why: Wrong - a T-score of -2.8 is well below the normal range
Wrong - osteopenia is defined as -1.0 to -2.5, and -2.8 exceeds this range
Correct - -2.5 or below without a fragility fracture is osteoporosis
Wrong - severe or established osteoporosis requires a coexisting fragility fracture, not stated here
exp: WHO DEXA classification: T-score -1.0 or above is normal, -1.0 to -2.5 is osteopenia, and -2.5 or below is osteoporosis; severe or established osteoporosis additionally requires one or more fragility fractures.

subject: Medicine
q: In a patient with severe hyperkalemia (serum K+ 7.2 mEq/L), which ECG change is the earliest and most characteristic?
why: Wrong - prolonged QT is more typical of hypocalcemia or hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia
Wrong - delta waves are a feature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, unrelated to potassium
Wrong - U waves are a classic finding of hypokalemia, the opposite electrolyte abnormality
Correct - peaked T waves are the earliest, most characteristic hyperkalemia change
exp: Tall, peaked (tented) T waves are the earliest ECG manifestation of hyperkalemia, appearing as serum potassium rises above roughly 5.5-6.5 mEq/L; with worsening hyperkalemia this progresses to PR prolongation, QRS widening, loss of P waves, and eventually a sine-wave pattern.

subject: Medicine
q: Involvement of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints with Heberden's nodes is characteristic of which joint disease, helping distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis, which classically spares the DIP joints?
why: Correct - DIP involvement with Heberden's nodes is the hallmark of osteoarthritis
Wrong - RA characteristically spares the DIP joints
Wrong - psoriatic arthritis can involve DIP joints but is typically associated with nail changes and dactylitis, not Heberden's nodes specifically
Wrong - gout classically presents as acute monoarticular podagra, not chronic DIP nodularity
exp: Osteoarthritis characteristically involves the DIP joints (producing bony Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes), whereas rheumatoid arthritis classically spares the DIP joints and instead targets the MCP and PIP joints and wrists symmetrically - a key clinical discriminator on exam.

subject: Medicine
q: A blood donor's serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, and anti-HBc negative. What does this pattern most likely represent?
opts: Immunity from prior hepatitis B vaccination
why: Correct - isolated anti-HBs without anti-HBc indicates vaccine-induced immunity
Acute infection shows HBsAg positive with IgM anti-HBc
Chronic infection shows persistent HBsAg with anti-HBc IgG
Window period is HBsAg negative with IgM anti-HBc positive - anti-HBc presence is the key differentiator from vaccine immunity
exp: Isolated anti-HBs positivity without anti-HBc indicates vaccine-induced immunity, since the vaccine contains only HBsAg and generates no anti-HBc; natural infection always produces anti-HBc (IgM acutely/in the window period, IgG after resolution or in chronic infection).

subject: Medicine
q: A patient has a low free T4 with an inappropriately normal (non-elevated) TSH. This biochemical pattern is most consistent with:
why: Primary hypothyroidism shows markedly elevated TSH with low T4
Correct - a low T4 without the expected compensatory TSH rise points to pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction
Subclinical hypothyroidism is elevated TSH with normal T4, the opposite pattern
Sick euthyroid syndrome shows low T3, variable T4, and normal/low TSH in a systemically ill patient without primary thyroid/pituitary disease
exp: In primary hypothyroidism, TSH rises appropriately as T4 falls (intact negative feedback); a low T4 with a normal/low TSH (failure of the expected compensatory rise) points instead to pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction, warranting pituitary imaging and assessment of other axes.

subject: Medicine
q: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with altered sensorium, severe dehydration, blood glucose 680 mg/dL, minimal ketones, and serum osmolality 340 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: DKA has significant ketosis/acidosis and is more typical of type 1 diabetes
Lactic acidosis shows a high anion gap with normal/low glucose, not this picture
Correct - classic HHS with minimal ketosis and markedly raised osmolality
Alcoholic ketoacidosis occurs with alcohol use and normal/low glucose
exp: HHS occurs typically in older type 2 diabetics with residual insulin - glucose is very high, ketosis is minimal/absent, and osmolality is markedly raised; the true differentiator from DKA is the degree of ketosis/acidosis and the larger free-water deficit, not the order of fluids vs insulin.

subject: Medicine
q: A 35-year-old IV drug user presents with fever, a new murmur, and vegetations >10 mm on echocardiography with Staphylococcus aureus grown from two separate blood cultures. How many major modified Duke criteria are met?
why: Correct - positive blood cultures plus echo evidence of endocardial involvement are both major criteria
Under-counts, criteria clearly are met
Under-counts, both blood culture and echo criteria are independently satisfied
Over-counts, only these two major criteria are present
exp: Modified Duke major criteria are positive blood cultures with a typical organism from two separate samples, and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement - both are satisfied here, meeting the definition of definite infective endocarditis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 40-year-old woman presents with symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands and morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour, improving with activity. Which serological marker is most specific for this condition?
why: RF is sensitive but less specific, positive in several other conditions
Correct - anti-CCP is highly specific (~95%) for rheumatoid arthritis
ANA is a screening test for SLE/connective tissue disease, not specific for RA
Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE, not RA
exp: Anti-CCP antibody is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, can predate clinical disease onset, and predicts a more erosive disease course - more specific than rheumatoid factor.

subject: Medicine
q: A 22-year-old with a history of recurrent childhood sore throats presents with exertional dyspnea and a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex in the left lateral position, with a loud S1. Which valve lesion is most likely?
why: Correct - rheumatic mitral stenosis classically causes this apical diastolic murmur with loud S1
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, not a rumbling apical murmur
Mitral regurgitation causes a pansystolic, not diastolic, murmur
Tricuspid stenosis is rare and best heard at the left lower sternal border, not the apex
exp: Mitral stenosis, most commonly due to rheumatic heart disease, presents with a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex with a loud S1, best heard in the left lateral position with the bell, often with an opening snap.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with a history of tuberculous pericarditis presents with ascites, raised JVP that paradoxically rises on inspiration, and a pericardial rim of calcification on chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Right heart failure from cor pulmonale
why: Tamponade classically causes pulsus paradoxus (fall in BP on inspiration), not a rise in JVP with inspiration, and does not calcify
Restrictive cardiomyopathy can mimic this clinically but doesn't typically show pericardial calcification
Cor pulmonale doesn't explain the JVP finding or calcification
Correct
exp: Kussmaul's sign — a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration — plus pericardial calcification (often post-tuberculous in India) is classic for constrictive pericarditis, where a thickened non-compliant pericardium limits diastolic filling.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient on long-term oral steroids for asthma abruptly stops them and presents in shock with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Blood is drawn for cortisol, but treatment must not be delayed pending the result. What is the immediate management?
opts: IV hydrocortisone plus IV fluids, started empirically without waiting for the cortisol result
Wait for the serum cortisol result before starting any steroid
Perform a formal ACTH stimulation test first, then treat based on result
why: Correct
Waiting for a cortisol result in a patient in shock risks death
Formal dynamic testing is deferred to after stabilisation
Fludrocortisone alone doesn't address the acute glucocorticoid deficiency; high-dose hydrocortisone itself has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect acutely
exp: Suspected Addisonian crisis is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate empirical treatment with IV hydrocortisone and aggressive fluid/dextrose resuscitation; treatment must never be delayed for laboratory confirmation given the high untreated mortality.

subject: Medicine
q: A 50-year-old man presents with bronze skin pigmentation, new-onset diabetes mellitus, and hepatomegaly. Iron studies show markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation above 45%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — classic bronze-diabetes triad with iron overload
Wilson disease presents with low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and neuropsychiatric features from copper overload, in a younger patient
Primary biliary cholangitis affects middle-aged women with pruritus and a cholestatic pattern, AMA positive, not iron overload
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes cirrhosis plus panacinar emphysema, unrelated to iron studies
exp: Hereditary hemochromatosis (usually HFE gene C282Y mutation) causes progressive iron deposition in the liver, pancreas, skin, heart, and joints, producing the classic triad of bronze diabetes (skin pigmentation plus diabetes) plus hepatomegaly/cirrhosis; markedly elevated transferrin saturation (>45%) is the best initial screening test, with ferritin used to gauge iron burden, and treatment is regular phlebotomy.

subject: Medicine
q: A 58-year-old man who had an anterior wall myocardial infarction three weeks ago now presents with pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, and a pericardial friction rub; ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and blood tests show a raised ESR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Reinfarction would show localized ST changes with a new troponin rise, not a rub with diffuse ST elevation and fever
Early peri-infarction pericarditis occurs within the first 1-4 days post-MI, much sooner than this 3-week presentation
Correct — delayed autoimmune pericarditis 2-10 weeks after MI is Dressler syndrome
Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain and dyspnea but not diffuse ST elevation or a pericardial rub, and lacks the temporal MI relationship
exp: Dressler syndrome is a delayed, immune-mediated pericarditis occurring typically 2-10 weeks after MI (or cardiac surgery/trauma), presenting with pleuritic chest pain, fever, pericardial rub, diffuse ST elevation, and raised inflammatory markers; it is thought to be an autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens exposed by necrosis, and responds to NSAIDs/aspirin, with steroids reserved for refractory cases and avoided early post-MI due to impaired healing.

subject: Medicine
q: A young woman presents with fatigue and elevated transaminases; investigations show hypergammaglobulinemia and a positive anti-smooth muscle antibody, with negative viral hepatitis markers. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Primary biliary cholangitis, treated with ursodeoxycholic acid
Autoimmune hepatitis, treated with corticosteroids plus/minus azathioprine
Hepatitis C, treated with direct-acting antivirals
why: Primary biliary cholangitis presents with pruritus and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP/GGT) with anti-mitochondrial antibody, not raised transaminases with anti-smooth muscle antibody
Wilson disease shows low ceruloplasmin and neuropsychiatric/KF ring findings, not anti-smooth muscle antibody
Correct — classic autoimmune hepatitis serology and first-line treatment
Hepatitis C requires positive viral markers, explicitly excluded here
exp: Autoimmune hepatitis (type 1) classically affects young to middle-aged women with a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury, hypergammaglobulinemia (raised IgG), and anti-smooth muscle antibody (or ANA) positivity after excluding viral causes; first-line treatment is corticosteroids, typically combined with azathioprine to allow steroid tapering, with liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis confirming diagnosis.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with a large pericardial effusion shows a fall in systolic BP of more than 10 mmHg during normal inspiration. What is this sign called, and what does it suggest?
opts: Pulsus parvus et tardus — aortic stenosis
why: Correct — inspiratory fall in SBP >10 mmHg reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence in tamponade
Pulsus alternans is beat-to-beat amplitude alternation with regular rhythm, seen in severe LV systolic dysfunction
Pulsus bisferiens is a double-peaked pulse of combined AS/AR
Pulsus parvus et tardus is a slow-rising, low-volume pulse of severe AS
exp: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in SBP >10 mmHg) reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence when the pericardium is non-compliant, classically seen in cardiac tamponade (also severe asthma/COPD) — a distinct bedside sign from Beck's triad.

subject: Medicine
q: A 50-year-old woman presents with progressive pruritus and fatigue; ALP is markedly elevated with a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — AMA positivity in a middle-aged woman with cholestatic pattern is classic for PBC
PSC is associated with ANCA and IBD with beaded strictures, not AMA
Autoimmune hepatitis shows a hepatocellular pattern with ANA/anti-smooth muscle antibody
Budd-Chiari presents with pain, ascites, hepatomegaly, not chronic pruritus with AMA
exp: Primary biliary cholangitis classically affects middle-aged women with pruritus, fatigue, and a cholestatic liver pattern (raised ALP/GGT); anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is positive in over 90% of cases and is highly specific.

subject: Medicine
q: A man extricated after being trapped under debris for 6 hours develops dark cola-colored urine, markedly elevated CK, and rapidly rising creatinine. What is the most likely mechanism of his AKI?
why: Pure pre-renal azotemia does not explain the cola-colored urine or markedly elevated CK
Correct — crush injury releases myoglobin causing pigmented cast nephropathy
AIN follows drug exposure with fever/rash/eosinophilia, not crush injury with elevated CK
Contrast nephropathy requires recent iodinated contrast exposure, not described
exp: Crush injury releases myoglobin from damaged muscle, which is directly nephrotoxic and precipitates as pigmented casts in the distal tubules (worsened by acidic urine), causing acute tubular necrosis — early aggressive IV fluids and urine alkalinization are key preventive measures in crush syndrome.

subject: Medicine
q: An elderly man presents with exertional syncope and angina; auscultation reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising, low-volume pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — syncope, angina, and pulsus parvus et tardus with carotid-radiating murmur is classic severe AS
Mitral regurgitation radiates to the axilla, not the carotids
HOCM murmur increases with Valsalva/standing, unlike AS, and doesn't classically cause parvus et tardus
Aortic regurgitation causes a diastolic murmur with a collapsing pulse, opposite of that described
exp: The triad of exertional syncope, angina, and dyspnea with a slow-rising, low-volume ('parvus et tardus') pulse and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids is classic for severe aortic stenosis — syncope and angina are poor prognostic markers indicating urgent valve replacement evaluation.

subject: Medicine
q: A 40-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis develops asymmetric swelling of the entire third finger ('sausage digit') with nail pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: RA classically causes symmetric small-joint polyarthritis without dactylitis
Gout presents as acute monoarthritis (classically first MTP), not a chronic sausage-digit pattern
Correct — dactylitis and nail pitting with psoriasis is classic psoriatic arthritis
Reactive arthritis follows GI/GU infection with the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis
exp: Dactylitis ('sausage digit,' from combined flexor tenosynovitis and joint inflammation) together with nail pitting/onycholysis in a patient with psoriasis is highly characteristic of psoriatic arthritis — a seronegative spondyloarthropathy that can cause the distinctive 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray in advanced disease.

subject: Medicine
q: A 42-year-old man has episodic headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating triggered by exertion; BP during an episode is 210/120 mmHg but normal between episodes. Which is the most sensitive initial biochemical test?
why: Urinary VMA is less sensitive than plasma metanephrines
Correct - highest sensitivity for pheochromocytoma screening
Serum cortisol screens Cushing syndrome, not pheochromocytoma
Clonidine suppression is a confirmatory test after positive biochemistry, not initial screen
exp: Plasma free metanephrines have ~96-100% sensitivity for catecholamine-secreting tumours and are the preferred first-line screening test over 24-hour urinary catecholamines/VMA (Endocrine Society Guidelines 2014).

subject: Medicine
q: A 24-year-old woman has daily spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-colored rash appearing with fever, arthralgia, sore throat, and markedly elevated serum ferritin. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why: SLE does not typically show quotidian fever with salmon rash and extreme hyperferritinemia
Correct - the classic tetrad defines adult-onset Still's disease
RA lacks the fever/rash/ferritin pattern
Reactive arthritis follows a GI/GU infection with a different triad
exp: Adult-onset Still's disease presents with the classic tetrad of quotidian spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-colored rash appearing with fever spikes, arthralgia/arthritis, and markedly elevated ferritin - a diagnosis of exclusion using the Yamaguchi criteria.

subject: Medicine
q: An elderly man with syncope has a regular but very slow pulse (32/min), intermittent cannon 'a' waves in the JVP, and variable intensity of S1 on auscultation. What is the most likely underlying rhythm abnormality?
why: AF gives an irregularly irregular pulse without cannon waves
First-degree block has a constant prolonged PR without AV dissociation
Correct - AV dissociation explains cannon a waves and variable S1
Sinus bradycardia has a normal consistent P-QRS relationship without cannon waves
exp: Intermittent cannon a waves plus a variable-intensity S1 in a patient with a very slow, regular pulse strongly suggests complete heart block with AV dissociation - atria and ventricles beat independently, so atrial contraction occasionally coincides with a closed AV valve, producing the cannon wave, and S1 intensity varies with the changing timing between the two.

subject: Medicine
q: A 60-year-old man with acute chest pain has ST-elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST-depression in I and aVL. Which coronary artery territory is most likely involved?
why: Correct - the inferior lead pattern localizes to RCA territory in most people
LAD occlusion causes anterior changes (V1-V4), not this pattern

LCx occlusion can occasionally cause inferior changes too in a left-dominant circulation (~10%), but the reciprocal depression pattern and the greater prevalence of right-dominant circulation make RCA the better answer here
Left main occlusion typically causes widespread diffuse ST depression with aVR elevation
exp: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL localizes an acute MI to the inferior wall, supplied by the right coronary artery in about 80-90% of people (right-dominant circulation) - right-sided precordial leads (V4R) should also be checked to rule out concurrent right ventricular infarction.

subject: Medicine
q: A 50-year-old man with heavy chronic alcohol use presents with jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and fever; his Maddrey discriminant function score is calculated as 38. What is the significance of this score in guiding management?
opts: Severe alcoholic hepatitis with high short-term mortality - consider corticosteroids
Score 32 or above indicates the patient needs immediate liver transplant evaluation only
Score 32 or above indicates mild disease - supportive care and abstinence alone suffice
Score 32 or above mandates pentoxifylline as first-line therapy
why: Correct - the classic threshold for considering corticosteroid therapy in severe alcoholic hepatitis
Transplant evaluation is a separate, later consideration requiring sobriety criteria, not indicated by this score alone
Wrong direction - a score of 32 or above is the severity threshold, not a marker of mild disease
Pentoxifylline is no longer recommended; the STOPAH trial (NEJM 2015) showed no survival benefit
exp: Maddrey's discriminant function (4.6 times the prothrombin time prolongation in seconds, plus serum bilirubin in mg/dL) of 32 or above identifies severe alcoholic hepatitis with significant short-term mortality risk and is the classic threshold for considering corticosteroid therapy - though the Lille score at day 7 is often used to assess steroid response and decide on continuation.

subject: Medicine
q: A young man develops conjunctivitis, asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limb, and urethritis 2-4 weeks after a chlamydial genitourinary infection. This classic triad describes:
why: Correct — classic post-infectious reactive arthritis triad
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic symmetric small-joint polyarthritis unrelated to a preceding urogenital infection
Psoriatic arthritis is linked to psoriatic skin/nail disease, not a preceding chlamydial infection
Ankylosing spondylitis presents with chronic inflammatory back pain, not this acute post-infectious triad
exp: Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy triggered by a preceding genitourinary (Chlamydia trachomatis) or gastrointestinal infection, classically presenting with conjunctivitis, urethritis, and asymmetric oligoarthritis, and strongly associated with HLA-B27.

subject: Medicine
q: A 19-year-old competitive athlete with a family history of sudden cardiac death has a systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border that intensifies with the Valsalva manoeuvre and on standing, and decreases with squatting. This is most consistent with:
why: Aortic stenosis murmur intensity is unaffected or decreases with reduced preload, not the reverse pattern described
Mitral regurgitation murmur increases with increased afterload (handgrip), not with Valsalva/standing
Correct — classic HOCM dynamic murmur behaviour
Mitral valve prolapse click/murmur timing shifts earlier with standing, but this is a different outflow pattern
exp: In HOCM, manoeuvres that reduce ventricular preload (Valsalva strain, standing) worsen left ventricular outflow obstruction and increase murmur intensity, while manoeuvres that increase preload/afterload (squatting, handgrip) reduce obstruction and soften the murmur — the opposite dynamic to most systolic murmurs.

subject: Medicine
q: A 28-year-old woman has had two episodes of blurred vision months apart; examination shows impaired adduction of the left eye on attempted right lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting right eye, and MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions. The likely diagnosis is:
why: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable, variable ophthalmoplegia without a fixed brainstem localisation pattern like INO
Correct — INO with relapsing course and periventricular lesions points to MS
Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia, not this eye-movement sign
Wernicke encephalopathy causes ophthalmoplegia with confusion/ataxia in thiamine deficiency, not this relapsing pattern
exp: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus, causing impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye on conjugate gaze; in a young adult with relapsing episodes and periventricular white matter lesions on MRI, it is a classic localising sign for multiple sclerosis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 68-year-old woman reports bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness for 6 weeks, worse in the morning and lasting over an hour, with an ESR of 90 mm/hr and normal muscle strength on testing. Before starting corticosteroids, she should specifically be asked about symptoms of which closely associated condition?
why: Rheumatoid arthritis is typically a symmetric small-joint polyarthritis, a different pattern from this proximal girdle presentation
Correct — the GCA overlap is the critical association to screen for
SLE is not the classic overlap condition with polymyalgia rheumatica
Fibromyalgia shows normal inflammatory markers, unlike this markedly raised ESR
exp: Polymyalgia rheumatica presents with bilateral proximal girdle pain and morning stiffness with markedly raised ESR/CRP but preserved muscle strength, and is closely associated with giant cell arteritis in up to 15-20% of cases; headache, jaw claudication, or visual disturbance must be actively sought before standard-dose steroids since GCA needs higher-dose steroids and urgent ophthalmology review.

subject: Medicine
q: A 24-year-old man presents with 4 months of low back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning, improves with exercise, and is associated with reduced chest expansion. He is HLA-B27 positive. What radiographic finding would confirm the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Sacroiliac joint erosion and fusion (sacroiliitis) with eventual bamboo spine
Subchondral cysts and osteophytes at the DIP joints
Erosive changes at the MCP and PIP joints with ulnar deviation
Punched-out lytic lesions in the skull
why: Correct, inflammatory sacroiliitis progressing to syndesmophyte formation and vertebral fusion
DIP osteophytes/cysts describe osteoarthritis, a degenerative pattern
MCP/PIP erosions with ulnar deviation describe rheumatoid arthritis, not HLA-B27 associated
Punched-out skull lesions suggest multiple myeloma, unrelated
exp: Inflammatory back pain (age under 40, insidious onset, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise, nocturnal pain) plus HLA-B27 positivity and reduced chest expansion is the classic ankylosing spondylitis vignette; MRI can detect sacroiliitis earlier than plain radiographs, which may take years to show bamboo spine changes.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old man with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes routine screening. His spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is elevated at 45 mg/g on two separate occasions, while his 24-hour total urine protein and serum creatinine remain normal. According to Mogensen's staging of diabetic nephropathy, what is the earliest clinically detectable stage he has reached?
why: Hyperfiltration is an early, subclinical GFR increase without detectable albuminuria
Overt nephropathy requires macroalbuminuria, not present here
Correct, persistent microalbuminuria with normal total protein defines Mogensen stage 3
ESRD requires significant GFR decline/dialysis dependence, not applicable
exp: Microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day or ACR 30-300 mg/g) is the earliest clinically detectable and, importantly, the most actionable stage of diabetic nephropathy - ACE inhibitors/ARBs and SGLT2 inhibitors at this stage can slow or even reverse progression, making annual microalbuminuria screening in all diabetics a key recommendation.

subject: Medicine
q: A 30-year-old woman reports progressive drooping of both eyelids that is minimal in the morning but worsens noticeably by evening, along with double vision and difficulty chewing tough food toward the end of meals. There is no sensory loss. Which finding on further testing would most support the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Improvement of ptosis after applying ice to the eyelids for 2 minutes
Elevated CSF protein with normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation)
Decreased corneal reflex on the affected side
why: Correct, cold improves neuromuscular transmission by reducing acetylcholinesterase activity, supporting myasthenia gravis
Albuminocytological dissociation is characteristic of Guillain-Barre syndrome, not myasthenia
Ascending weakness with areflexia describes GBS, not this fatigable pattern
Reduced corneal reflex suggests a trigeminal or facial nerve lesion, not myasthenia
exp: Myasthenia gravis classically causes fatigable weakness that worsens with sustained use/through the day and improves with rest - ocular and bulbar symptoms are the most common presenting features; the ice-pack test is a simple, safe bedside alternative to the edrophonium/Tensilon test, and anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) antibody testing confirms the diagnosis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use is brought to the emergency department confused, with horizontal nystagmus, bilateral abducens nerve palsy, and a wide-based unsteady gait. Before administering intravenous dextrose for suspected hypoglycemia, which additional treatment should be given to prevent worsening of his neurological state?
why: Correct, Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia triad) results from thiamine deficiency; glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen it
Folic acid deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, not this triad
B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, a different and more chronic picture
Magnesium deficiency can cause tremor/seizures but is not the specific concern here
exp: In any patient with suspected thiamine deficiency (alcoholics, malnourished, hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged fasting/bariatric surgery), thiamine must be given before or together with IV dextrose - glucose before thiamine is a classic exam trap and real clinical hazard, since glucose metabolism further depletes marginal thiamine stores and can precipitate frank Wernicke's encephalopathy.

subject: Medicine
q: A cirrhotic patient has albumin 2.6 g/dL, INR 1.9, bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, diuretic-controlled ascites, and no encephalopathy. Which score is used to prioritize this patient for liver transplant?
why: Wrong — Child-Pugh is useful for prognosis/staging but is not the primary transplant-allocation tool.
Wrong — Ranson's criteria assess acute pancreatitis severity, unrelated to transplant priority.
Wrong — Glasgow-Blatchford scores upper GI bleed risk, not transplant priority.
Correct — MELD is the objective score used for liver transplant waitlist prioritization.
exp: MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) uses bilirubin, INR, and creatinine (or MELD-Na with sodium) to predict 3-month mortality and is the objective, continuous score used to prioritize patients on the liver transplant waiting list. Child-Pugh (albumin, bilirubin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) is more useful for prognostication and surgical risk staging of cirrhosis, but MELD is the transplant-allocation standard.

subject: Medicine
q: A 15-year-old presents with tremor, dysarthria, a golden-brown corneal ring, and elevated liver enzymes with low serum ceruloplasmin. What is the diagnosis, and what confirms it?
opts: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; serum AAT level
why: Wrong — hemochromatosis causes bronze diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and arthropathy, not a corneal ring or tremor as presenting features.
Wrong — autoimmune hepatitis does not classically cause a corneal ring or these neurological signs.
Correct — this tetrad with low ceruloplasmin is classic Wilson disease, confirmed by 24-hour urinary copper.
Wrong — alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver disease with early emphysema, not neurologic or corneal findings.
exp: Wilson disease (autosomal recessive, ATP7B gene mutation causing a copper transport defect) presents with hepatic and neuropsychiatric features (tremor, dysarthria, parkinsonism), a Kayser-Fleischer ring (copper deposition in Descemet's membrane), and low serum ceruloplasmin. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion (or hepatic copper on biopsy); first-line treatment is chelation (D-penicillamine or trientine) plus zinc.

subject: Medicine
q: A 50-year-old woman has dry eyes, dry mouth, and bilateral parotid swelling for 8 months, with positive anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
why: Wrong — SLE can also carry anti-Ro/La antibodies, but the dominant sicca-plus-parotid-swelling presentation here is specific to Sjögren, not lupus's typical multi-organ pattern.
Correct — sicca symptoms with parotid swelling and anti-Ro/La positivity is classic primary Sjögren syndrome.
Wrong — rheumatoid arthritis does not classically present primarily with sicca symptoms and parotid swelling as the leading feature.
Wrong — systemic sclerosis features skin thickening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and GI dysmotility, not primarily sicca symptoms with anti-Ro/La.
exp: Primary Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune exocrinopathy causing keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, often with parotid gland enlargement, driven by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands. Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies are characteristic. A key long-term complication to screen for is MALT (marginal zone) lymphoma, suggested by persistent parotid enlargement or monoclonal gammopathy.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old man presents with a saddle-nose deformity, recurrent haemoptysis, and rapidly progressive renal failure. Serology is strongly positive for c-ANCA. Which antigen does this c-ANCA target?
why: MPO is the p-ANCA antigen, associated with microscopic polyangiitis, not classic c-ANCA-positive GPA.
Correct — PR3 is the c-ANCA target antigen in GPA.
Anti-dsDNA is characteristic of SLE, not ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse systemic sclerosis, unrelated to this presentation.
exp: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with the triad of upper respiratory disease including saddle-nose deformity, lower respiratory involvement with nodules or haemoptysis, and rapidly progressive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. It is strongly associated with c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3, which correlates with disease activity, distinguishing it from microscopic polyangiitis which is p-ANCA or MPO-associated.

subject: Medicine
q: Which autoantibody is most specific for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, as opposed to the limited cutaneous (CREST) variant?
why: Correct — anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse cutaneous SSc with a higher risk of interstitial lung disease
Anti-centromere antibody is specific for limited/CREST scleroderma, not diffuse disease
Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with Sjogren syndrome and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block, not scleroderma
Anti-Jo-1 is specific for antisynthetase syndrome (myositis with ILD), not scleroderma
exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and a higher risk of interstitial lung disease; anti-centromere antibody instead marks the limited cutaneous (CREST) variant with a milder, more indolent course.

subject: Medicine
q: A 4-year-old boy presents with failure to thrive, polyuria, and rickets-like bone deformities. Investigations show hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypophosphatemia, glucosuria with a normal blood glucose, and generalized aminoaciduria. On an oral acid load, urine pH falls below 5.5. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
opts: Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis with Fanconi syndrome
why: Distal RTA cannot acidify urine below 5.5 despite systemic acidosis, and does not cause Fanconi-pattern glucosuria/aminoaciduria
correct — Fanconi triad plus a urine pH that falls appropriately below 5.5 localises the defect to the proximal tubule
Type 4 RTA is hyperkalemic (aldosterone-related), not associated with Fanconi syndrome
Bartter syndrome causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis with Fanconi features
exp: The combination of glucosuria with normoglycemia, phosphaturia, and generalized aminoaciduria is Fanconi syndrome — failure of proximal tubular reabsorption — the hallmark of proximal (type 2) RTA. Unlike distal (type 1) RTA, distal acidifying capacity is intact in type 2 RTA, so urine pH CAN fall below 5.5 once the filtered bicarbonate load drops below the reduced proximal reabsorptive threshold — the key discriminator on an acid-load test.

subject: Medicine
q: A 30-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease develops fever, tachycardia, and altered sensorium after an emergency appendectomy. In managing this thyroid storm, which sequence of drug administration is correct?
opts: Iodine solution first, followed an hour later by propylthiouracil
Propranolol alone is sufficient without antithyroid drugs
Radioactive iodine ablation as the first emergency step
Propylthiouracil first, followed at least one hour later by iodine solution
why: Wrong — iodine before the thionamide risks supplying substrate for a surge in new hormone synthesis.
Wrong — beta-blockade controls adrenergic symptoms but does not block hormone synthesis or release.
Wrong — radioactive iodine has delayed onset and is contraindicated in acute storm.
Correct — propylthiouracil/methimazole must precede iodine by at least one hour.
exp: In thyroid storm, propylthiouracil (or methimazole) must be given at least one hour before iodine. Giving iodine first can fuel a surge in new hormone synthesis before the thionamide blocks organification; giving the thionamide first ensures iodine's acute Wolff-Chaikoff inhibitory effect on hormone release predominates.

subject: Medicine
q: A 60-year-old man started on ciprofloxacin for a UTI develops fever, an erythematous rash, and a rising creatinine on day 10. Urinalysis shows white cell casts, sterile pyuria, and eosinophils on Hansel stain. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: ATN shows muddy-brown granular casts, not WBC casts or eosinophiluria
Correct — fever, rash, eosinophiluria, and a temporal drug link are the classic (if often incomplete) triad of AIN
PSGN follows streptococcal infection with RBC casts and low complement, not this picture
RPGN shows an actively nephritic sediment (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs) with rapid GFR loss over days-weeks, not eosinophils
exp: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis classically presents with fever, rash, and eosinophilia/eosinophiluria plus sterile pyuria with white cell casts; fluoroquinolones, beta-lactams, and NSAIDs are recognised triggers, and the culprit drug must be stopped promptly.

subject: Medicine
q: A 45-year-old man wakes up with sudden drooping of the left side of the face. He cannot close his left eye or wrinkle his forehead on that side, and drools from the left angle of the mouth. There is no limb weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Bell's palsy (left lower motor neuron facial palsy)
Right middle cerebral artery stroke with contralateral facial weakness
why: Correct — whole-face involvement including forehead, no limb weakness, points to an LMN (facial nerve) lesion, i.e. Bell's palsy.
A left MCA stroke would spare the forehead (UMN pattern) and usually cause right-sided limb weakness, not left facial droop with intact limbs.
A right MCA stroke causing contralateral (left) facial weakness would also spare the forehead and typically comes with left limb weakness — neither fits here.
MS can rarely cause isolated facial palsy but is a much less common cause than Bell's palsy and usually has other CNS signs.
exp: Forehead sparing distinguishes an upper motor neuron (cortical/stroke) facial palsy from a lower motor neuron one: the frontalis has bilateral cortical representation, so a cortical lesion spares the forehead while a facial-nerve (LMN) lesion — as in Bell's palsy — involves the entire half of the face equally, including the forehead.

subject: Medicine
q: A 22-year-old woman reports malaise, low-grade fever, and left arm claudication for 6 months. Blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg in the right arm but unrecordable in the left; the left radial pulse is absent and a bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. ESR is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — young female, limb claudication, pulse/BP asymmetry, and elevated ESR fit Takayasu arteritis
Kawasaki disease is a childhood vasculitis causing coronary artery aneurysms, not adult limb claudication
Giant cell arteritis affects the temporal/cranial arteries in patients typically over 50, with headache and jaw claudication
Buerger's disease affects young male smokers with distal small/medium vessel disease, not proximal large-vessel pulse asymmetry
exp: Takayasu arteritis ("pulseless disease") is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis typically affecting young Asian women, causing limb claudication, unequal pulses/BP between limbs, bruits, and a raised ESR from active aortitis. It is the classic vignette for a young woman with asymmetric pulses.

subject: Medicine
q: A 40-year-old woman has resistant hypertension on three antihypertensives and is found to have persistent hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is elevated and plasma renin activity is suppressed, giving a markedly raised aldosterone-renin ratio. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension with palpitations/sweating/headache and raised metanephrines, not primarily a high-aldosterone/low-renin picture
Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with a HIGH renin, giving a low/normal ratio, not a raised one
Correct - resistant hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis and a raised aldosterone-renin ratio is classic for primary hyperaldosteronism
Cushing syndrome can cause hypokalemia only at very high cortisol levels and typically shows normal-to-low aldosterone/renin, not a raised ratio
exp: Resistant hypertension with unprovoked hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and a high aldosterone with suppressed renin (raised aldosterone-renin ratio, the screening test of choice) is classic for primary hyperaldosteronism - most often an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia; a positive screen is followed by confirmatory testing and adrenal imaging/vein sampling.

subject: Medicine
q: A 58-year-old man presents with bilateral pedal edema and frothy urine. Investigations show urine protein 4.5 g/24h, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, and normal renal function. Renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits on silver stain, and granular IgG/C3 deposits on immunofluorescence. What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's workup?
opts: Minimal change disease is confirmed on this biopsy; start steroids without further workup
This is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; look for a preceding throat or skin infection
This is membranous nephropathy; screen for an occult secondary cause such as malignancy, hepatitis B, or lupus given the patient's age
This is FSGS; test for HIV given the biopsy pattern
why: This biopsy shows GBM spikes and subepithelial deposits, not the normal light microscopy of minimal change disease
PSGN shows subepithelial humps with an acute nephritic picture and a preceding infection, typically in children — not this histology
Correct
FSGS shows segmental glomerulosclerosis on light microscopy, not GBM spikes/subepithelial deposits
exp: Membranous nephropathy is the classic cause of nephrotic syndrome in older adults, with subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits and granular IgG/C3 on immunofluorescence. Most adult cases are primary, but secondary membranous nephropathy — from an occult solid-organ malignancy, hepatitis B, SLE, or drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine) — must always be actively excluded in older patients, since management differs (treating the underlying cause versus immunosuppression).

subject: Medicine
q: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain, rapidly progressive ascites, and tender hepatomegaly. Liver function tests show markedly elevated transaminases. Doppler ultrasound of the abdomen shows absent flow in the hepatic veins with hypertrophy of the caudate lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Viral hepatitis does not produce this Doppler pattern of hepatic venous outflow obstruction or selective caudate hypertrophy
Portal vein thrombosis affects the portal (inflow), not hepatic venous outflow, and does not give this Doppler picture
Correct
Chronic decompensated liver disease develops gradually, not as an acute presentation with this specific vascular finding
exp: Budd-Chiari syndrome results from obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (hepatic veins or IVC), classically presenting with the triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and tender hepatomegaly; the caudate lobe hypertrophies because it drains directly into the IVC via separate short veins, sparing it from the obstruction. Risk factors are hypercoagulable states — OCP use, pregnancy, polycythaemia vera, and other myeloproliferative/thrombophilic disorders — and Doppler ultrasound showing absent/reversed hepatic venous flow is the key confirmatory finding.

subject: Medicine
q: In a young patient with severe aortic regurgitation, which peripheral sign refers to a rapidly rising and abruptly collapsing arterial pulse felt at the wrist?
why: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP, seen in tamponade or severe asthma, not AR
Correct — water-hammer pulse is the classic sign of severe AR's wide pulse pressure
Pulsus alternans (alternating strong/weak beats) signals severe LV systolic dysfunction
Pulsus parvus et tardus is the slow-rising pulse of severe aortic stenosis, the opposite hemodynamic picture to AR
exp: Corrigan's (water-hammer) pulse reflects the wide pulse pressure of severe aortic regurgitation — a large stroke volume ejected into a low-resistance regurgitant diastolic circuit gives a rapid upstroke and rapid collapse. Contrast with pulsus parvus et tardus of aortic stenosis.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient has recurrent sweating, tremor, and confusion that resolve promptly after eating. During a supervised fast, plasma glucose falls to 45 mg/dL with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide, and symptoms resolve immediately after glucose is given. This constellation is known as?
why: Somogyi phenomenon is rebound morning hyperglycemia after nocturnal hypoglycemia, a diabetes-management concept, not a diagnostic triad
Dawn phenomenon is early-morning hyperglycemia from a physiological GH/cortisol surge, unrelated to this symptom complex
Zollinger-Ellison relates to gastrinoma and peptic ulcers, not hypoglycemia
Correct — Whipple's triad defines and confirms a genuine hypoglycemic disorder
exp: Whipple's triad — symptoms of hypoglycemia, a documented low plasma glucose during those symptoms, and relief after glucose correction — confirms true hypoglycemia and is the diagnostic prerequisite before pursuing an insulinoma work-up.

subject: Medicine
q: A 35-year-old man develops rapidly progressive, ascending, symmetric limb weakness two weeks after an episode of acute diarrheal illness. Deep tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally, and CSF examination shows markedly elevated protein with a normal cell count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Transverse myelitis typically causes a sensory level and sphincter involvement with spinal cord MRI changes, not albuminocytologic dissociation
MS is a CNS demyelinating disease with CSF oligoclonal bands and pleocytosis, not typically post-infectious ascending weakness
Poliomyelitis causes asymmetric flaccid paralysis with CSF pleocytosis, not albuminocytologic dissociation
Correct — GBS classically follows Campylobacter jejuni diarrhea with ascending symmetric weakness, areflexia, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation
exp: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy, classically preceded by Campylobacter jejuni diarrhea, causing ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cell count) after the first week of illness.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old man presents with acute monoarticular pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy shows needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent. What is the diagnosis?
why: Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, not needle-shaped/negatively birefringent as described here
Septic arthritis would show organisms/high WBC on Gram stain and culture, not crystals
Correct - monosodium urate, needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals with classic podagra presentation
Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory, typically polyarticular and symmetric arthropathy without crystal deposition
exp: Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition - needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on polarized microscopy of synovial fluid. Pseudogout (CPPD disease) shows rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals instead. First MTP joint involvement (podagra) is the classic presentation of acute gouty arthritis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 28-year-old man develops rapidly ascending symmetrical limb weakness and areflexia two weeks after an episode of diarrhoeal illness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is most likely to show:
