opts: Elevated protein with markedly raised neutrophils
Elevated protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)
why: A markedly neutrophilic, high-protein CSF suggests bacterial meningitis, not Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Normal protein with lymphocytic pleocytosis is the pattern of viral (aseptic) meningitis, not Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Low glucose with high protein points to bacterial or tuberculous meningitis, where glucose consumption occurs - Guillain-Barre CSF glucose is normal.
Correct - the classic albuminocytologic dissociation of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
exp: Guillain-Barre syndrome, frequently post-infectious (classically after Campylobacter jejuni diarrhoeal illness), classically shows albuminocytologic dissociation on CSF analysis - markedly raised protein from nerve root inflammation but a normal or only mildly raised cell count - which distinguishes it from infectious meningitis patterns and is a core discriminator on NEET PG.

subject: Medicine
q: A hospitalized patient's serum creatinine rises from a baseline of 0.8 mg/dL to 1.7 mg/dL over 36 hours, with urine output of 0.4 mL/kg/hr for the last 8 hours. What KDIGO AKI stage is this?
why: Correct - a 2.1x baseline creatinine rise meets Stage 2 (2.0-2.9x)
Stage 1 criteria are exceeded by the creatinine ratio here, so Stage 1 undercalls severity
Stage 3 requires 3x baseline or more, creatinine 4.0 mg/dL or more, RRT initiation, or oliguria/anuria criteria, none of which are met
AKI criteria are clearly met by both the creatinine rise and the oliguria
exp: KDIGO AKI staging uses whichever criterion, serum creatinine or urine output, gives the higher-severity stage: here creatinine has risen to 2.1x baseline within the window (Stage 2 range is 2.0-2.9x baseline), while urine output of less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 8 hours meets only Stage 1 on its own - the higher of the two, Stage 2, is assigned.

subject: Medicine
q: A patient with clinical features of Cushing syndrome shows suppression of serum cortisol with high-dose dexamethasone but not with low-dose dexamethasone. What is the most likely source of the excess cortisol?
why: An ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor typically shows no suppression even with high-dose dexamethasone.
Adrenal adenomas are ACTH-independent, so cortisol does not suppress with dexamethasone at any dose.
Adrenal carcinomas are also ACTH-independent and characteristically non-suppressible.
Correct - a pituitary corticotroph adenoma retains partial feedback sensitivity and suppresses with high-dose but not low-dose dexamethasone.
exp: The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test differentiates the cause of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome: pituitary corticotroph adenomas (Cushing disease) retain partial feedback sensitivity and suppress cortisol by more than 50 percent with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg), whereas ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors and ACTH-independent adrenal tumors typically show no suppression. Low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress in all causes of Cushing syndrome and is used only to confirm the syndrome, not to localize it.

subject: Medicine
q: A 26-year-old woman with two prior second-trimester pregnancy losses presents with acute left leg swelling; Doppler confirms DVT. Her aPTT is prolonged and fails to correct on a 1:1 mixing study. Which antibody is most likely responsible?
why: Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE (especially renal disease), not this thrombosis/pregnancy-loss pattern
Correct - lupus anticoagulant explains the non-correcting mixing study plus obstetric and vascular morbidity
Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) marks diffuse systemic sclerosis, not this presentation
Anti-Jo-1 marks antisynthetase syndrome/dermatomyositis with ILD, not thrombosis
exp: Recurrent pregnancy loss plus venous thrombosis plus a prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct on mixing study is the classic triad of antiphospholipid syndrome, driven by lupus anticoagulant, which paradoxically prolongs the in-vitro aPTT while promoting in-vivo thrombosis; diagnosis needs the revised classification criteria with confirmatory testing 12 weeks apart.

subject: Medicine
q: Which histological lesion on renal biopsy is characterized by normal light microscopy, diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy, and dramatic steroid responsiveness in children with nephrotic syndrome?
why: Correct — the classic steroid-responsive lesion of childhood nephrotic syndrome
FSGS shows focal sclerotic lesions and is often steroid-resistant
Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern, mainly in adults, usually steroid-resistant
MPGN shows immune deposits and low complement with a tram-track appearance
exp: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome, classically normal on light microscopy with diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement only visible on electron microscopy, and shows dramatic (over 90%) response to an 8-week course of oral steroids — this steroid responsiveness itself is a bedside diagnostic clue that often avoids the need for biopsy in typical childhood cases.

subject: Medicine
q: A 32-year-old man presents with bilateral flank pain, hypertension and hematuria. His father died of renal failure. Ultrasound shows multiple bilateral renal cysts of varying sizes along with a few hepatic cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Simple cysts are usually solitary or few, without a family history or extrarenal cysts
Correct — bilateral renal cysts, hepatic cysts, hypertension, and family history point to ADPKD
Medullary sponge kidney causes collecting duct ectasia and nephrocalcinosis, generally a benign, non-familial course
Von Hippel-Lindau is associated with renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma, a much rarer explanation than ADPKD for this presentation
exp: ADPKD (PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16 in about 85% of cases; PKD2 on chromosome 4, milder and later-onset) presents in adulthood with bilateral enlarging renal cysts, hypertension, hematuria, flank pain, and a positive family history. Extrarenal manifestations include hepatic cysts (the commonest), intracranial berry aneurysms, and mitral valve prolapse — screen first-degree relatives with renal ultrasound and counsel about intracranial aneurysm screening if there is a family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage.

subject: Medicine
q: A 19-year-old man develops gross, cola-coloured haematuria on the same day he develops sore throat and fever, resolving over 2-3 days; he has had two similar episodes in the past year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis — latent period after pharyngitis
IgA nephropathy — synpharyngitic haematuria coinciding with upper respiratory infection
Alport syndrome — hereditary nephritis with sensorineural deafness
Thin basement membrane disease — persistent microscopic haematuria only
why: PSGN has a latent period of 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis, not synchronous onset
Correct — synpharyngitic recurrent gross haematuria coinciding with URI is classic for IgA nephropathy
Alport syndrome presents with persistent haematuria plus sensorineural deafness and lenticonus, not described here
Thin basement membrane disease causes persistent asymptomatic microscopic haematuria, not recurrent gross episodes tied to URI
exp: IgA nephropathy classically presents with gross haematuria synchronous with an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic), often recurrent — this timing is what distinguishes it from post-streptococcal GN, which has a 1-3 week latent period after pharyngitis before haematuria appears.

subject: Medicine
q: A 58-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites develops progressive oliguria and creatinine rising to 2.8 mg/dL over 48 hours despite stopping diuretics and receiving albumin 1 g/kg/day for two days; urine sediment is bland, urine sodium is low, and there is no shock. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Renal reserve assessment with a furosemide challenge
why: A diuretic challenge in a volume-contracted cirrhotic can worsen renal perfusion and is neither diagnostic nor therapeutic here.
Hemodialysis is reserved for refractory cases unresponsive to vasoconstrictor-albumin therapy or as a bridge to transplant.
Vasoconstrictors are only effective combined with albumin, which restores effective arterial volume; norepinephrine alone is inadequate.
Correct — terlipressin (or noradrenaline in ICU settings) plus albumin is the first-line vasoconstrictor strategy for HRS-AKI.
exp: Hepatorenal syndrome-AKI is a diagnosis of exclusion in cirrhosis with ascites: creatinine rise without shock, nephrotoxins, structural kidney disease, or response to 2 days of albumin (1 g/kg/day) and diuretic withdrawal. First-line treatment is a vasoconstrictor (terlipressin, or noradrenaline in ICU settings) plus 20% albumin to improve effective circulating volume and renal perfusion; TIPS or liver transplant are definitive options.

subject: Medicine
q: A 58-year-old man with known cirrhosis is brought in lethargic and disoriented to time and place, with a noticeable personality change over the past day. Flapping tremor is elicited on wrist extension, and serum ammonia is elevated. Which grade of hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven criteria) does this presentation most likely represent?
why: Grade I lacks asterixis and shows only subtle mood/attention changes
Correct
Grade III involves marked confusion, incoherent speech, and stupor — more severe than described
Grade IV is coma, inconsistent with a patient who is conversing, even if slurred
exp: West Haven Grade II hepatic encephalopathy is characterized by lethargy, disorientation, personality change, and the presence of asterixis (flapping tremor). Grade I has only trivial lack of awareness with no asterixis; Grade III has marked confusion with incoherent speech and a drowsy-but-rousable patient; Grade IV is frank coma unresponsive to stimuli.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old man on hydralazine for 18 months for resistant hypertension develops new arthralgia, pleuritic chest pain, and a malar-sparing rash. ANA is positive, anti-histone antibody is positive, and anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exp: Drug-induced lupus - classically from hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, and increasingly TNF-alpha inhibitors - presents with arthralgia/arthritis, serositis, and mild rash, but nephritis and CNS involvement are rare, unlike idiopathic SLE. It is characterised by a positive ANA and anti-histone antibody (>95% sensitivity) with typically negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm, and resolves within weeks to months of stopping the offending drug.

subject: Medicine
q: A 24-year-old man develops polyuria (6-7 L/day) and excessive thirst 48 hours after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. Serum sodium is 152 mEq/L, and urine osmolality remains inappropriately low despite water deprivation. Administration of desmopressin leads to a marked rise in urine osmolality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
exp: Post-pituitary-surgery polyuria with hypernatremia and dilute urine that responds to desmopressin confirms central DI (ADH deficiency). Nephrogenic DI would show no or blunted response to desmopressin; psychogenic polydipsia presents with low-normal serum sodium; cerebral salt wasting causes hyponatremia, not hypernatremia.

subject: Medicine
q: Which single clinical parameter best differentiates SIADH from cerebral salt wasting, both of which present with hyponatremia, natriuresis, and inappropriately concentrated urine in a neurosurgical patient?
exp: SIADH is a euvolemic (or mildly hypervolemic) hyponatremia managed with fluid restriction, while cerebral salt wasting is hypovolemic hyponatremia from renal salt loss requiring salt and volume replacement -- giving fluid restriction to a CSW patient worsens hypovolemia, so correct volume assessment is the practical bedside differentiator despite both sharing similar labs. Some texts note this distinction can be clinically difficult in practice.

subject: Medicine
q: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis on imaging, and hypokalemic metabolic acidosis; urine pH remains persistently above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exp: Distal (type 1) RTA is caused by failure of alpha-intercalated cells to secrete H+, so urine pH stays inappropriately above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis; resulting hypocitraturia and alkaline urine predispose to calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis. Proximal (type 2) RTA can drop urine pH below 5.5 once the reduced bicarbonate reabsorptive threshold is exceeded, and rarely causes stones. Type 4 RTA causes hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. Bartter syndrome causes hypokalemic alkalosis with normal urine acidification.

subject: Medicine
q: A 50-year-old woman has Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly limited to the fingers and face, telangiectasia, and dysphagia. Which antibody is most specific for this limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis?
exp: Anti-centromere antibody is highly specific for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome — Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia), whereas anti-Scl-70 correlates with diffuse cutaneous disease and a higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis.

subject: Medicine
q: A 60-year-old man on carbamazepine for 6 months presents with mild lethargy and nausea but is hemodynamically stable with no edema. Labs show serum sodium 125 mEq/L (gradual onset), low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, and urine sodium greater than 40 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?
exp: Carbamazepine is a recognized cause of drug-induced SIADH; in mild-to-moderate chronic hyponatremia without severe neurological symptoms, fluid restriction (roughly 800-1000 mL/day) is the appropriate initial measure — hypertonic saline is reserved for severe or rapidly progressive symptomatic hyponatremia, and overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.

subject: Medicine
q: A 52-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever and diffuse abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count of 380 cells/mm3. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
exp: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm3 in a cirrhotic with ascites, without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. Empirical treatment is IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) plus IV albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3) — albumin reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk and improves survival. Norfloxacin is for secondary prophylaxis, not acute treatment, and surgical exploration is not indicated.

subject: Medicine
q: A 52-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and combing her hair over 3 months, a violaceous rash over the upper eyelids, and scaly erythematous papules over the knuckles. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. Given her age, which additional evaluation is most important at this diagnosis?
exp: This is dermatomyositis (proximal myopathy plus heliotrope rash plus Gottron's papules plus raised CK). Adult-onset dermatomyositis, especially after age 40, carries a significantly increased risk of occult malignancy (ovary, lung, GI, breast, non-Hodgkin lymphoma), so age-appropriate cancer screening is mandatory at diagnosis and for 3-5 years after.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old presents 2 hours after the onset of crushing chest pain with ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. The nearest catheterisation laboratory is a 4-hour transfer away. Best immediate reperfusion strategy?
exp: If primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, thrombolysis should be given without delay and the patient transferred afterwards. Waiting for troponin when the ECG is already diagnostic only wastes salvageable myocardium.

subject: Medicine
q: A 26-year-old with childhood rheumatic fever has exertional dyspnoea. Auscultation reveals a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Diagnosis?
exp: Loud S1 with an opening snap and a rumbling mid-diastolic apical murmur is mitral stenosis. A SHORTER S2-to-opening-snap interval indicates more severe stenosis, because a higher left atrial pressure forces the valve open sooner.

subject: Medicine
q: A young man with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, blood glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.10 and ketonuria. His pulse is 124/min with BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the first step in management?
exp: Fluid resuscitation precedes insulin in DKA: the patient is profoundly volume depleted, and starting insulin first drives glucose and potassium intracellularly, worsening shock and precipitating dangerous hypokalaemia. Potassium is added once it falls below 5.3 mEq/L with confirmed urine output.

subject: Medicine
q: Linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence microscopy is characteristic of which condition?
why: Membranous shows granular subepithelial 'spike and dome' IgG deposits, not linear
Correct — smooth continuous linear GBM staining is the immunologic hallmark of anti-GBM disease
PSGN shows granular 'starry sky' IgG/C3 deposits
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not linear GBM staining
exp: Linear IgG (and often C3) staining along the GBM is the immunofluorescence hallmark that separates anti-GBM disease from every other glomerulonephritis, which show granular deposits instead; anti-GBM antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen and can cross-react in the alveolar basement membrane, producing the pulmonary hemorrhage-plus-RPGN picture of Goodpasture syndrome.

subject: Medicine
q: Which autoantibody in systemic sclerosis is most strongly associated with diffuse skin disease and scleroderma renal crisis?
why: Marks limited cutaneous/CREST disease, low renal-crisis risk
Marks diffuse disease with high ILD risk, not the strongest renal-crisis link
A Sjogren/lupus marker, not specific to scleroderma
Correct — carries the highest associated risk of scleroderma renal crisis among SSc-specific antibodies
exp: Scleroderma antibody subsets predict phenotype: anti-centromere marks limited/CREST disease; anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse disease with pulmonary fibrosis risk; anti-RNA polymerase III marks diffuse disease with the highest risk of scleroderma renal crisis, so a positive result should prompt closer home blood pressure monitoring.

subject: Medicine
q: Which electrolyte disturbance is characteristic of acute digoxin toxicity and correlates with mortality risk?
why: Correct — acute Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition causes hyperkalemia that tracks with mortality
Hypokalemia potentiates chronic toxicity, not the acute-overdose finding
Hypercalcemia potentiates arrhythmogenicity but is not the characteristic acute finding
Hyponatremia is not a recognized feature of digoxin toxicity
exp: In acute digoxin poisoning, Na+/K+-ATPase blockade pushes potassium out of cells, so the serum potassium level at presentation is a validated mortality predictor (Bismuth criteria); this is the opposite of chronic toxicity, where hypokalemia often precipitates it.

subject: Medicine
q: Superior vena cava syndrome in an adult is most commonly caused by which malignancy?
why: A recognized but less common cause
An infrequent cause of SVC obstruction
Correct — lung cancer accounts for the large majority of malignant SVC syndrome
A rare cause
exp: Roughly three-quarters of malignant superior vena cava syndrome is due to bronchogenic carcinoma compressing or invading the SVC from the right paratracheal/hilar region; the syndrome should trigger urgent chest imaging and tissue diagnosis before, not instead of, symptomatic treatment.

subject: Medicine
q: In a cirrhotic patient with altered mental status, serum ammonia level is best used for which purpose?
opts: To grade the severity of encephalopathy
To confirm the diagnosis in a typical presentation
To support the diagnosis when the picture is atypical
As a routine screen in every cirrhotic with altered sensorium
why: Ammonia does not correlate with West Haven grade
A typical presentation is diagnosed clinically; ammonia adds nothing and a raised level is not specific
Correct — a raised level supports HE when the picture is atypical; a normal level calls for re-evaluation
Routine ammonia testing is not recommended; HE is a clinical diagnosis
exp: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; serum ammonia neither grades severity nor is required when the clinical picture is typical, but a markedly elevated level can support the diagnosis in atypical presentations, and a normal level should prompt evaluation for alternative causes of encephalopathy.

subject: Medicine
q: Metformin is temporarily withheld before administration of iodinated contrast media primarily because of the risk of which complication?
why: Correct — accumulated metformin after contrast-induced AKI can precipitate life-threatening lactic acidosis
Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy
Metformin does not cause the nephropathy itself; it is the resulting AKI that creates risk
Hepatotoxicity is not a recognized metformin risk
exp: The metformin-contrast precaution exists because metformin is renally cleared and accumulates if contrast triggers acute kidney injury, precipitating type B lactic acidosis; current practice individualizes the hold based on baseline eGFR and contrast dose.

subject: Medicine
q: ACE inhibitors can precipitate acute kidney injury in a patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis through which mechanism?
opts: Direct tubular toxicity of the drug
Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction needed to maintain glomerular filtration pressure
why: ACE inhibitors are not directly nephrotoxic to tubular cells
Contributory at most, not the principal mechanism
AIN is an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction, unrelated here
Correct — this hemodynamic mechanism is the classic cause of ACEI-induced AKI in bilateral RAS
exp: In critical bilateral (or solitary-kidney) renal artery stenosis, GFR is preserved by angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction; blocking this with an ACE inhibitor collapses filtration pressure and precipitates AKI. A creatinine rise of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor should prompt evaluation for renovascular disease.

subject: Medicine
q: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign of malignancy) is classically associated with which underlying cancer?
why: RCC is classically linked to erythrocytosis/hypercalcemia, not Trousseau's sign
Correct — mucin-driven tissue factor release makes pancreatic cancer the classic association
Not the classic association
Gastric cancer can cause hypercoagulability but is not the classic teaching answer
exp: Trousseau's sign of malignancy — recurrent, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis — reflects tumor-driven hypercoagulability and is classically taught with pancreatic adenocarcinoma; unexplained venous thromboembolism in an older adult should prompt occult-malignancy screening focused on the pancreas.

subject: Medicine
q: Beck's triad of hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and elevated jugular venous pressure is classically associated with which condition?
why: Correct — reflects acute compression of the heart limiting diastolic filling in tamponade
Constrictive pericarditis is chronic; its signs are Kussmaul's sign and a pericardial knock, not this acute triad
Causes hypotension and distended neck veins but with tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds
Causes shock and elevated JVP but not muffled heart sounds
exp: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP) is taught as the acute bedside recognition pattern for cardiac tamponade, though in practice all three are present in only a minority of cases, so pulsus paradoxus and echo remain essential to confirm the diagnosis.

subject: Medicine
q: Charcot's neurologic triad of nystagmus, intention tremor, and scanning (staccato) speech is classically described in which condition?
why: Wilson disease causes tremor/dysarthria with a Kayser-Fleischer ring and low ceruloplasmin, a different picture
Friedreich ataxia presents with ataxia, areflexia, pes cavus, and cardiomyopathy
Correct — the classic cerebellar-plus-brainstem triad of MS
Parkinson disease features bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting (not intention) tremor
exp: Charcot's triad is a historically named but still exam-tested cerebellar pattern (nystagmus, intention tremor, scanning speech) associated with multiple sclerosis; current MS diagnosis relies on the McDonald criteria (MRI dissemination in space and time), not this triad alone.

subject: Medicine
q: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites undergoes therapeutic large-volume paracentesis, with 6 litres of ascitic fluid removed. To prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, which additional measure is most appropriate?
opts: IV albumin, 6–8 g per litre of total ascitic fluid removed
why: Diuretics do not address the intravascular volume depletion from rapid fluid removal
Correct — the recommended peri-procedure prophylactic measure for large-volume taps
Terlipressin is reserved for hepatorenal syndrome or variceal bleeding, not routine prophylaxis
FFP is not indicated for volume replacement and adds unnecessary transfusion risk
exp: Large-volume paracentesis (>5 L) without albumin replacement risks post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction — a fall in effective arterial volume that can precipitate renal impairment, dilutional hyponatremia, and faster re-accumulation of ascites — so guidelines recommend IV albumin 6–8 g per litre of the total volume removed whenever more than 5 litres is tapped.
